en: The Vyāsaparipṛcchāsūtra, Volume One, translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was traveling along the Gaṅgā River in the region of Ayodhyā.
On the bank, he was together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.

Those bhikṣus had accomplished what was to be done; they had exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), were free from hindrances, and being non-retrogressive, they had transcended existence. Diligently engaged in meditation and recitation, they sat cross-legged wherever they were—some on the ground, two following one another, discussing the Dharma according to the rules, moving in groups like geese or mandarin ducks; some in empty huts, and some at the roots of trees—all of them practicing dhyāna, able to grasp the radiance of the Tathāgata’s Dharma and the majestic deportment of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there was an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas together with him; those bodhisattvas possessed immeasurable merit, and their fame was heard everywhere.

In that place, there were also countless hundreds of thousands of various groves of trees, filled with the sounds of many *jīvañjīvaka* birds, peacocks, geese, other birds, and swarms of bees, as well as the branches and leaves of *sālakalyāṇī* trees hanging down and spreading about.
In such a place, the desire-mind, indolence, fondness for sleep, and yawning are all entirely absent; there are always immeasurable fragrant scents and exquisite flowers.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You bhikṣus, you should always practice with diligence, perform what ought to be done, and maintain the precepts in right conduct."

At that time, the World-Honored One was together with the Venerable Ānanda, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, the Elder Śāriputra, the Elder Bakkula, the Elder Revata, Ajñātakauṇḍinya, and other great śrāvakas, conversing joyfully.
At that time, there was a manifestation of light in the western quarter, resembling the orb of the sun.
Then Ānanda, because his outflows were not yet exhausted, saw that sign and immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is this, World-Honored One?"
"In the western direction, there is a place where the light of flame-colored radiance possesses great majesty and power?
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"

In this world, there was a seer possessing the five supernatural powers named Viśvāmitra—the son of the Gandhārī woman Gārgī—who had five hundred seers as his retinue. Residing there, he diligently practiced asceticism; fasting and observing the precepts, his body was so emaciated that he barely survived, making the constant recitation of scriptures his sole adornment.
Their names were:
the youth Asita Rishi, Nārada, Sāṃkṛtya, Parvata, Nādāyana, Nāgamitra, Naśanji, Rāṣṭrapāla, Nāsatya, and Rādhā; these great ṛṣis followed one another as they walked along.

At that very moment, the sage Vyāsa also beheld the World-Honored One in the forest grove, surrounded by a retinue of many thousands of bhikṣus—his faculties tamed and supple, his mind tranquil, dwelling in meditative concentration, free from desire, and at peace.
Having seen the Buddha, the seer Vyāsa reflected and thought:
"This person must be the Omniscient One; his fame is heard everywhere, and he must surely be one who does not speak falsely."

Thus, the Tathāgata is endowed with supreme physical form; the perfection of his marks is exceedingly rare and unprecedented in the world, for such physical characteristics are sublime, wondrous, and extraordinary.

In this way, the World-Honored One renounced the pleasures of kingship and the sovereign wealth and enjoyments of a wheel-turning monarch as if discarding poisoned food; having abandoned all sixty thousand court ladies, who were of the most exquisite beauty, he then went forth into homelessness and dwelt in the forest.
Among the assembly of sages was one named Nārada; upon seeing the World-Honored One, his heart was filled with joy, and he praised the Tathāgata with these sublime verses:
"Within this forest of blue trees, whose radiance is like molten gold?
It is as pure as lapis lazuli, like the sun emerging from the mountain clouds."

When that great seer and the assembly of seers heard these words, their hearts were filled with joy and their eyes opened wide; they all joined their palms, desiring to go toward the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Bhikṣus, do you see these seers of Jambudvīpa, who have bound their hands and feet, suspended themselves from trees, observed fasts without eating, wear garments of tree bark, and lie upon the dust?"

If they are upon rocks, some take their food with both hands, closing them together and then opening them to eat; others subsist on air; some observe the fast by not eating for fifteen days, while others observe the fast by not eating for a month; their heads, beards, hair, and nails all grow long and sharp.

Recite and chant at the three times—dawn, midday, and evening. Possessing the wealth of noble lineage and the wealth of merit, first consecrate the objects with mantras and then place them within the fire as an offering to Agni.

Lying on the ground, some were in the open air, some under trees; some slept with their hands tied above them as they hung from a tree, some slept squatting in this manner, and some slept thus in the water.

Some roast their bodies with the five heats; some lie down pressing their bodies against fire to scorch themselves; some lie down in the wind beneath a great flame; some lie upon thorns; and some have their bodies scorched by the sun.

Undergoing suffering while seeking merit, they deceive themselves by remaining content with whatever position they attain; their minds are satisfied and delighted by their superior lineage, thereby distancing themselves from unsurpassed wisdom.
"O bhikṣus!
This great seer was unable to know the essential way out of birth and death.
Because of desire and delusion, he was reborn within existence; yet he considered his own practice to be correct, unaware that it was actually wrong."
At that time, those bhikṣus took refuge in the Tathāgata and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Our holy life is truly complete; we have lived in harmony and accord, and have attained liberation from birth and existence.”

Those great ṛṣis, such as Viśvāmitra and others—out of fear born from the majestic power of the Arhat, gazing upon him with composure and clarity, their minds filled with reverence and their attention fixed in right mindfulness—accompanied by their retinues of ṛṣis, bound their long hair together into a single bundle, draped their bodies with fine woven cords, and though their complexions were not white, they maintained a dignified physical bearing. Their eyes were both yellow, their hair was free of oiliness, knotted and matted together in many clumps; holding trident staffs in their hands, they carried water-pots that were the most unsightly in the world, and they were all skilled in various modes of speech, their words being perfectly accomplished.
Traversing through the air, he arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
You should know this matter: for what causes and conditions have I, together with my retinue, come here today?"
The Buddha said,
"Great Seer! All that has come into being and all phenomena— I know them all."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Such a Great Sage, surrounded by a host of sages, possesses right knowledge, manifold knowledge, subtle knowledge, and exhaustive knowledge; he knows yet remains unafraid, with his long hair left untended.”
"Who is this person?
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
This is the ṛṣi named Vyāsa. He is the author of the Brahmanical dharma;
he composed the four Vedas, was well-versed in the science of phonetics (śikṣā), and knew various scripts.
At that time, when all those arhats had seen the great seer Viśvāmitra, they reflected thus:
"That man undergoes suffering and exerts himself in maintaining his precepts; what will he thereby attain?"
"This Vyāsa has not yet attained liberation from the suffering and afflictions of saṃsāra.
Those arhats thought thus:
"This Vyāsa has come to the Buddha's presence; what questions will he pose?"
"Is this a question concerning causes and conditions,
or is it a question concerning non-self?
Then Viśvāmitra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The appearance of a Buddha in the world is rare.
Now that this assembly of sages has gathered here in harmony, I have a few difficult questions to ask; I pray only that you will remain for a moment and explain them to me."
The Buddha said, "Great Seer!
Ask whatever you wish; whatever you have in mind may all be asked, and I shall explain it for you."
Then Viśvāmitra asked,
"World-Honored One,
what is giving?"
For what reason does one practice giving?
What is the meaning of "giving"?
And who is a donor?
In what sense is one a donor?
How is it that a person who gives is not a donor?
And how can one be called a donor even when giving nothing?
How is it that after death the merit of giving follows one?
What is the nature of this merit of giving?
Does it have a physical form or mass that can be perceived?
Is it invisible?
Where does the merit of the donor’s gift reside—
is it in the recipient?
Is it for the sake of the donor?
How can one obtain the fruit of merit by making offerings to stupas and the like after the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa?
Once the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, who is there to receive [the offering]?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great seer Vyāsa, saying:
"The Dharma you inquire about is exceedingly subtle; your eloquence is inconceivable, for you are able to ask such a question."

At that time, the Elder Śāriputra—his hair white and his face wrinkled, with eyebrows drooping so as to cover his face—raised one eyebrow and drew in a long breath, contemplating and reflecting with deep attention.
Having seen him, he said:

"This great seer and lord, Viyasa, possesses great renown—known by all people and spoken of by all people. How could he not know that [this question] is like that of a worldly, foolish child, lacking in wisdom? Having already set aside the teaching of causes and conditions, set aside the teaching of non-self, and [discussed] various profound dharmas and various virtues with speech that accords with true knowledge, why does he now ask such a question regarding the dharma of giving?"
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding this question asked by the great seer Vyāsa concerning the karmic fruit of giving, I too am able to explain it.”
The Buddha said,
“Ānanda, this is not the right time.”
"If one were to ask the Tathāgata about what the śrāvakas have said, this would not be appropriate.
Cease, Ānanda! There is no such principle."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Whatever intention the seer may have in asking his question, I am able to explain it and satisfy his mind.”
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra, your words were too hasty; you did not reflect upon them with your mind.”
"Elder Śāriputra!
Do not speak such words; this is inconsistent.
If it were so, then my śrāvaka disciples would be inconsistent."
If someone were to come and ask me, and I were to speak as a śrāvaka, it would be inconsistent;
then some people would say: "That Tathāgata is not omniscient."
There may be those who say:
"The seer Vyāsa went to question the Tathāgata, but being unable to explain it himself, he sent a śrāvaka to speak.
Or there may be those who say:
"That Tathāgata possesses the view of self-conceit (asmimāna), yet he does not speak of it himself.
At that time, those bhikṣus conceived pure faith toward the World-Honored One and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"That Great Sage has asked; the Tathāgata is able to explain and to sever his doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke to the Great Sage Vyāsa, saying:
"Listen to the retribution of giving, and furthermore, to the various divisions of giving."
In what sense is it called "giving" (*dāna*)?
Having given, one consumes for oneself and attains purification; because the fruit of the gift is transformed [into merit], it is called giving.
For what reason is one called a "donor" (*dānapati*)?
O Great Seer, please listen to this question:

Suppose a person possesses wealth and, having conceived faith, entrusts that property to another person to take to a foreign land. That person takes the goods to the foreign land and gives them as a gift;
when that person performs the act of giving, the owner of the wealth gains merit, not the one who actually gave the gift.
One who is sent by another may hold an object to offer, yet is not the master of the relinquishment.
If a person gives their own property with their own hand, they are both the master of the relinquishment and the donor.
“Great Seer, you should know that there are thirty-three kinds of impure giving. What are these thirty-three?
First, there are those who, with a crooked mind and inverted views, lack pure faith yet relinquish their wealth and goods; such giving is not pure giving.”
"Second, there are those who give away wealth and goods for the sake of repaying a debt of gratitude; this is not true giving.
Third, there are those who give away wealth and goods without a heart of compassion; this, too, is not true giving."
"Fourth, there are those who give away wealth and goods out of lustful desire; this is also not giving.
Fifth, there are those who give things to fire; this is also not giving."
"Sixth, there are those who give things to water; this is also not giving.
Seventh, there are those who give rise to such a thought:
'I shall give things to the king, hoping that the king will recognize and remember me.'"
"Thus, giving away objects in such a manner is not pure generosity.
Eighth, there are those who give away their possessions to others out of fear of bandits; such a gift is also not pure generosity."
Furthermore, there are five kinds of giving away objects that are not pure gifts.
What are these five?
First, giving poison is not a pure gift.
"Second, giving weapons is not pure giving.
Third, teaching others to take meat and give it away is not pure giving.
Fourth, giving to beings who have been gathered under one's influence with the expectation that they will provide labor after being harmonized and nurtured is not pure giving."
"Fifth, there are those who give away wealth and goods for the sake of fame; this is not pure giving.
Fourteenth, there are those who give things to performers for the sake of song and dance; this is not pure giving."
"Fifteenth: There are those who, at the end of the year or the end of the month, squander and dissipate their wealth and goods;
this is not pure giving. Sixteenth: There are those who give away their wealth and goods for the sake of houses and dwellings; this is not giving."
"Seventeenth: There are those who, due to the influence of a 'good friend,' receive the wealth of others and bestow it upon another person;

this is not pure giving. Eighteenth: There are those who, regarding fields or houses, or heaps of grain or heaps of wheat that are consumed by deer, birds, mice, and the like, give them away without a pure mind; this is not pure giving."
"19. There are those who give goods to craftsmen for the purpose of learning a craft; such giving is not pure generosity. 20.
There are those who, having physical illness and fearing the end of their lives, relinquish goods to a physician; this is not pure generosity."
"Twenty-first: If a person, having struck or reviled another, later feels regret and shame and gives them material goods, this is not pure giving."
"Twenty-second: If, after having given a gift, a person conceives doubt in their mind, thinking, 'Will there be a reward or not?
such a giver does not practice pure giving."
"Twenty-third: If, after having given a gift, one feels regret and distress in the heart, such a giver does not perform pure giving.
Twenty-fourth: If, after having relinquished an object to another, one reflects thus:
'If anyone were to take my property, it would all belong to me; it was held by me.'"
Such a donor does not perform pure giving.
Twenty-fifth: if, after having given, a person reflects thus:
"The merit of such giving accrues solely to my own person and does not belong to others."
"Such a donor does not practice pure giving. Twenty-sixth:

if a person gives away their possessions when they are old; or when they are no longer in middle age but at a later time, afflicted by illness, death is imminent, the pulses and joints are about to fail, and they are oppressed by suffering as they enter the path of death; if they give away their possessions at such a time without a pure mind and without a mind of faithful purity—when the messengers of Yama see them and break into laughter, while their brothers and kinsmen weep and wail in grief—this is not pure giving."
"Twenty-seventh: If a person gives away material things for the sake of fame, thinking:
'In this way, my name shall be heard throughout other lands—that I am the great master of almsgiving in such-and-such a country and such-and-such a city.'"
"Such giving as that is not pure giving. Twenty-eighth:

if one harbors mutual hatred and jealousy toward others, and upon seeing them give away their possessions and practice extensive generosity, feels conceit and cannot endure it; if, out of envy for them, one gives away possessions as a gift, this is not pure giving."

"Twenty-ninth: Because of coveting another's wife or for the sake of one's lineage, one gives up pearls, gold, silver, diamonds, lapis lazuli, silk, garments, and cotton-wool bedding; such giving of things is not pure generosity."
"Thirty: There is a person who reflects thus when relinquishing things to others:
'I have no children, yet I am immensely wealthy and possess abundant riches; I ought to relinquish these things and practice generosity.'"
Giving in such a manner is not pure giving.
"Thirty-first: Furthermore, if there is someone who gives rise to discrimination in their mind, thinking thus:
'If I give to this person, there will be merit; if I give to that person, there will be no merit.'
"Such a giver does not perform pure giving. Thirty-second:

if a person gives alms by excluding those who are impoverished, whose clothes are tattered, or who are soiled with grime, and instead bestowing them upon those who already possess great abundance and wealth, this is not pure giving."
"Thirty-third: If there is another person who, desiring fine flowers and fruits, gives away their possessions, this is not pure giving.

Great Seer, you should know that these thirty-three defiled forms of giving involve the relinquishing of wealth; the retribution for such giving is like sowing seeds in salty soil—they rot and fail to grow."
"Great Seer, you should know that such a person is not one who does not practice giving, yet they do not obtain its fruit and retribution.
Furthermore, Great Seer, it is like a person who,
having obtained seeds from wherever they may be, plants them in a wasteland."

When that seed-element and the earth-element depend upon one another, they require the rain from heaven; yet if the seed is damaged or decayed, although a sprout may emerge, it will not produce flowers or fruit.
This failure to obtain flowers and fruit in the case of this portion of giving is likewise so.
Having spoken thus, the ṛṣi Vyāsa joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the Omniscient One, has spoken of the retribution of giving through appropriate discourse, thereby bringing benefit and peace to all sentient beings."
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
How is it that giving does not lose its fruit and retribution?
There are those who maintain the precepts and those who do not; if one gives to both, what is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said:
"Great Seer!
Listen now well to the teaching on the retribution of giving."
If one possesses a mind of faith that gives away everything, it is called giving;
if one practices giving without fear of the future and practices giving without disparaging others, it is truly called giving.

"Great Seer, you should know that if there is another person who does not discriminate among fields of merit—whether they possess the precepts or lack them—and with a mind of faith and open eyes, having given rise to a sense of affection, gives away material things as an offering, their mind constantly and universally takes all sentient beings as its object."
"Great Seer, you should know that such a person is a donor.
Great Seer, you should know that there are five kinds of giving by which a donor fulfills their practice.
What are these five?"

First, giving at the proper time; second, giving to those who practice the Way; third, giving to the sick and to those who attend to them; fourth, giving to those who are vessels for the Dharma; fifth, giving to those who wish to travel to foreign lands.
These are the five kinds.
“Furthermore, there are five kinds of giving.
What are these five? First, the gift of Dharma;
second, the gift of the necessities of life; third, the gift of dwellings; fourth, the gift of lamps; and fifth, the gift of fragrant garlands.”
"These are the five kinds.
The Great Seer asked:
"What is pure giving?"
The Buddha said:
"Great Seer!

If a person possesses faith and, based on sentient beings, gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of equanimity, and a mind of joy, and relinquishes material things as an act of giving, all of that is pure."
If one aspires for liberation, such giving is pure.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of unsurpassed giving.
What are these five?

First, giving to the Tathāgata is unsurpassed; second, giving to the Saṃgha is unsurpassed; third, giving to those who are vessels of the Dharma is unsurpassed; fourth, giving to one's parents is unsurpassed; fifth, giving to kings who have lost their thrones or to those who are impoverished is unsurpassed.
Giving in such a manner constitutes the supreme gift.
"To give to the elderly, the solitary, and those in urgent distress is a great act of giving;
to utterly abandon one who has been bound and is about to be executed because a king is enraged is a great act of giving;
and to disregard one's own life and relinquish one's wealth in order to rescue others from various emergencies is a great act of giving."
To give medicine to the sick is a great act of giving;
to give at the proper time to the Saṃgha who are fully endowed with the precepts is a great act of giving;
to give to one who seeks wisdom is a great act of giving.
If one gives to animals that are in fear—namely, such animals as owls, crows, and deer—it is a great act of giving;
if one gives to a person in urgent poverty according to their needs, it is a great act of giving.
"Great Seer, you should know that this is a great gift and should always be practiced with right cultivation.
Furthermore, if there is someone who, being sent by another, holds an object to give as an offering, they too possess a pure mind and likewise obtain the merit of giving."
Furthermore, if there is someone who, upon seeing another person practicing giving, gives rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), they too shall obtain the merit of giving.
Whether it be one who exhorts others to give or one who provides the objects for giving—all such persons shall obtain great merit.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
Regarding what you asked:
'After the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, how can one obtain the reward of merit by making offerings to his stūpas and so forth?'"

"O Great Seer, you should listen: if there is a person who provides offerings after I have entered parinirvāṇa, and if there is another person who provides offerings to me while I am still in the world and have not yet entered parinirvāṇa, the meritorious rewards obtained by these two are equal."
Why is this? The Dharmakāya Tathāgata is not the rūpakāya.
Whether one makes offerings now in the present, or makes offerings after my parinirvāṇa, because the mind is impartial, the merit obtained is no different.
“Great Seer, you should know that it is like a Wheel-Turning King who issues a universal decree to all his realms:
‘All people, from this day forward, must no longer kill living beings, nor shall you utter false speech.’”
There was a certain person who, having heard the king’s command, although he did not see the king, faithfully observed the king’s command.
Although such a person did not personally serve the body of the wheel-turning monarch, the king felt joy toward that person in his heart.
Such a person, having well protected the king’s command, will, through the karmic cause and condition of the wholesome deed of not killing, be reborn in a celestial realm.
"Great Seer, you should know: if a person does not perceive the physical form of my body and does not study the words of the precepts, what can they possibly attain?"
If a person sees me yet harbors wrong views in their heart—just as Devadatta did—they shall enter hell;
however, it should be known that those who have well-trained themselves in the precepts after my entry into parinirvāṇa are superior.

"Great Seer, you should know that my physical form is now superior; having realized all-knowledge, I am able to cause even faithless sentient beings to train in the precepts, let alone those who possess faith."
"If a person makes offerings after I have entered parinirvāṇa, it is no different from making offerings while I am present.
Great Seer, listen to what you asked:
'Where does the merit of giving reside?'"
"Regarding such a question: it is like a thicket of reeds growing so densely and thickly that when fire breaks out within it, if rain falls, the fire is immediately extinguished right there.
In this very way, whatever donor’s gift is complete and their merit is harmonized, once the rain of faith has fallen, that merit remains with the donor and does not go elsewhere."
Great Seer, you should know that the merit of such giving does not exist as a gathered place, nor does it have a physical form.

Once such a gift has been given, even when the giver’s life has ended, the merit of the gift does not depart; it follows them like a shadow follows a form. This is called the giver receiving the fruit of the reward for their merit.
The fruit of merit is never lost; it is like sugarcane, reeds, or peaches: if they are not pressed, one does not obtain their juice, but by pressing them, one obtains it.
It is not that the juice is visibly present and gathered within the sugarcane or the grapefruit, nor does it reside in the joints, yet it is not without juice.
In this very way, when material wealth is given as a gift, the fruit of such giving does not abide in the hand of the donor, nor in his heart, nor in his belly;
yet the fruit of that giving does not depart from the donor, just as that juice does not depart from the sugarcane or the grapefruit.

In this way, the retribution for such giving does not depart from the donor; it is not received as long as it is not yet matured, nor can the retribution for the gift be obtained until the life-force (āyuḥ-saṃskāra) has reached its end.
"It is like the seed of the Nyagrodha, the king of trees: its seed is minute, and when planted in the earth, it cannot be seen; only when the tree begins to grow does it become visible."
The merit of the donor’s giving is likewise so: it is only when the conditions harmonize and ripen that one obtains the fruit of retribution.

"It is like a merchant who brings very little with him when entering a great city—yet through the virtues of that city, what was a small amount for making a living becomes a great deal once fully realized."
Giving is also like this: although the act of giving may be small at the time it is performed, the resulting merit and reward are great.
Furthermore, just as a honeybee gathers the nectar from flowers without damaging them, so it is with the donor.
"Who is the donor who gains the power of the fruit and retribution from whatever gift is given?
It is thus, O Great Sage!
It is the donor's power of merit resulting from the act of giving."
Regarding the term "donor" (dānapati): one is called a donor because of giving from oneself.
What is meant by a "recipient" (pratigrahaka)?
One is called a recipient because they receive what is given by others and are able to digest the goods of others.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'merit from giving'?
It is called merit because it can rescue, protect, and bring fulfillment within the world, and because it enables one to obtain the bodies of humans and devas.
"As for what is called 'another world,' it refers to the successive transmission of birth until one reaches a body in a future life; therefore, it is named 'another world.
At that time, the Rishi Viśvāmitra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
I have abandoned doubt and am resolved regarding the portion of the gift; yet, World-Honored One, I still have further doubt:
how does this consciousness circulate within the body?
“How does consciousness perceive?
How does it give rise to craving and delight toward the body?
The Buddha said:
“Great Seer!

It is like a king dwelling within a city who, fearing an enemy army, first constructs moats and trenches encircling the city; he prepares provisions of food, as well as bows, arrows, swords, shields, and various weapons; he gathers many brave and capable warriors and erects banners of heroic men; he also assembles many young and strong men and provides them with rations; and he commands the taverns to prepare much fine wine.”
He gathered the renunciants to offer them gifts and sustenance, winning over the people with excellent wealth and goods.
Having done so, he raised his voice and commanded:
"Remain steadfast and do not move; each of you must prepare your weapons, holding bows and arrows in hand and wearing armor upon your bodies, drawing your swords and remaining on guard."
Having thus exhorted them, the enemy army arrived with many elephants and horses.
At that time, the king comforted his troops, saying:
"Exert yourselves and do not fear. If there are any parts of the city walls that are not secure, you must guard them well, doing so every day."
"In this way, until his merit is exhausted, he is destroyed by the enemy host; in an instant, defeated and scattered, he abandons his kingdom and departs.

Consciousness is also like this: dwelling as the king within the city of the body among the various sense bases (*āyatana*), it perceives that the army of impermanence is about to arrive and gives rise to fear."

Immediately, one constructs the trench of faith, levels the precipitous banks of the realms, dons the armor of mindfulness, exerts diligent vigor, takes the treasury of Dharma as wine, and skillfully tames the horse of the mind.
At that time, he thus commanded and instructed those who have entered [the city], telling them to perform what is to be done:

"If an army of the impermanent—whether possessing great power or immeasurable strength—should come to press upon the city of the body, quickly don the armor of generosity, quickly take up the sword of wisdom, properly install the mechanism of shame and remorse, and maintain the precepts of reality; in this way, remain steadfastly established."
Then that army of impermanence suddenly arrives; they immediately engage in battle, clashing with one another.
The army of impermanence prevails, and consciousness departs.
Just as a king abandons his city and departs, so too is consciousness.

When the aggregates of the composite body and the elements have been destroyed, and the six sense bases have been lost, it abandons that city of the body, just as a ruined-city king abandons his city and flees.
Just as that king, having thus abandoned his city, takes refuge in another city;
so too is consciousness: having abandoned this body, it takes up another body.
One should know that this consciousness is no different from the king.
At that time, the seer Vyāsa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In this regard, how does consciousness know whether the body possesses merit or lacks merit?”
How does this consciousness come to know thus:
"I am casting off this body"?
The Buddha said, “Great Seer!
It is like a traveler who encounters a great body of water on the road; as the waters are overflowing, he boards a large raft in order to cross over them.”

As that water grows long, its waves surge and churn in disorder, and it becomes exceedingly turbid and teeming with malevolent creatures—namely, *nāgaras*, *śuśumāras*, water serpents, and vicious turtles.
There was a great, violent wind blowing in turbulent swirls; by relying upon that raft, he reached the other shore safely and without deficiency.
Having thus escaped from those evil waters and that place of great terror, the man circumambulated the raft three times and conceived a feeling of attachment toward that wooden raft.
Once love had arisen in his heart, he reflected thus:
"Excellent! This raft will enable me to cross over such a great flood of water."
"Thus it is, Great Seer!
Furthermore, there are other beings of merit who, once their bodies have died, their consciousness forms this thought:
'By means of this body of mine, I have been born in a good realm, having arisen among the devas.'"
I have gained no small benefit from this human body; this dying body of mine is like a sturdy raft, capable of enabling me to cross the great waters of the evil realms.
This body of mine is a great good fortune and deserves to be honored; such a body has not deceived me, for amidst the perils of birth and death, it has granted me a celestial abode.
Having reflected thus, he immediately conceives a sense of affection for that body.
Regarding that body as a raft, once he has abandoned it, he departs for the next world.
"Furthermore, if there is a person whose body lacks merit, that person's mind-consciousness is like someone crossing a great body of water on a rotting raft; yet that wooden raft may emerge or sink."
That person, filled with fear, gives rise to doubt and anxiety, thinking: "I shall die before long.

Such a person, relying upon that rotten raft, experiences great terror as he is carried downstream against the current until he reaches a place abounding in lions, tigers, and other fierce beasts—a place of immense dread—only after which he finally succeeds in crossing over.
Once that person has thus crossed over, they give rise to a mind of anger toward that rotten raft and revile it, saying:
"This is perverse and evil; this water is surging and overflowing, with many turbulent and foul waves."
"Why has it come to pass that I have reached such a wretched place?
What power have I gained from this rotten raft?
Thinking thus, he abandons the raft immediately.
"So it is, so it is. The mental consciousness of sentient beings, relying upon a body lacking merit, flows downward and regresses, falling into hell.
They revile this body, speaking thus:"
"What power have I gained?
I have already reaped such an evil body as a result of my karma.
Such a body is like a *kaṇa*; I carry this body as if I were carrying a *kaṇa*."
"I am now utterly wretched; because of this, my rotting body shall reach the gates of hell, just as a lotus is bound by its own fibers.
"Great Seer, you should know that consciousness is also like this."
If one possesses wholesome merit, it is like relying on a sturdy raft to cross over birth and death;
if one lacks merit, it is like relying on a rotten raft and thus falling into the evil realms.
One should understand that these two types of bodies—one possessing merit and one lacking merit—are to be known in this way.
Furthermore, when this consciousness transmigrates, relinquishing this body and obtaining a second body, during the first seven days within the womb, it thus recollects and knows:
"I have passed away from such-and-such a place and have come here."
They are also able to recollect and know the actions performed in the past, thinking:
"I performed this action.
If they have performed a wholesome action, joy arises in their mind.

Once he had taken up residence within the womb, his mother’s heart was filled with joyful laughter, and she possessed many superior signs: her face bore a smile, and no freckles or blemishes appeared upon it; her countenance was of a radiant hue; in whatever movement she made, she frequently used her right foot to tread firmly upon the ground; without any apparent cause, she would rub her right side with her hand; she took delight in fresh white garments, and when she wore them, they appeared magnificent and beautiful.
When sentient beings possess such meritorious consciousness, these signs appear while they dwell within their mother’s womb:
"Great Seer, you should know that if one possessed of merit were to have such consciousness, during the first seven days after taking birth, they would be able to recollect and know:
'I have passed away from such-and-such a place and have come to be born here.'"
They are also able to recollect and know the actions performed in the past, thinking thus:
"How did I commit these evil deeds?
As they reflect in this way, their minds become filled with sorrow and anxiety.
Because of the distress in her mind, the mother’s physical appearance manifests outwardly.

When that being—lacking merit and lacking virtue—dwells within the mother’s womb, external signs appear: her body becomes foul-smelling and emaciated; she is filled with sorrow, anxiety, and affliction; she cannot stop spitting repeatedly; and her face is furrowed with her eyes glaring in anger.
When such sentient beings are first within the womb, they cause misfortune and illness to fall upon that family.
When such beings of evil karma and no merit are about to emerge from the womb, they may either kill their mother or die within the womb itself.
“Sentient beings lacking merit possess such signs as these.
At that time, the Rishi Vyāsa addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!
"When this primary consciousness first enters the womb, what does it recollect?
What does it perceive and know?
The Buddha said:
"Great Sage!
That consciousness, upon first arising, forms such a recollection:

'I see places of play and delight within the groves, palaces, and multi-storied towers; winding rivers and waters, vast and level marshlands, and various dwellings; here in Jambudvīpa are many beloved people, parents, and brothers.'"
Having seen this, they give rise to an intense heart of affection.
Merit is gathered together and mutually sustained; there is one who possesses the gift and one who receives the gift.
He is able to know the events of his past lives; he recollects immeasurable hundreds of births and immeasurable thousands of births, and his consciousness thus repeatedly recalls them.
Having recollected this, his heart gave rise to love and joy, and he was able to know thus:
"This mother of mine has already served as my mother during five hundred past lifetimes."
Having thus reflected in his mind, he no longer conceived any longing for that place of birth; his mind became free from desire, and he formed this thought:
"I have undergone birth and death here again and again; from now on, I shall no longer undergo birth and death, nor shall I be subject to existence."
When he had spoken thus, the seer Vyāsa asked:
“World-Honored One!
Can such a consciousness become free from desire within the cycle of birth and death?”
The Buddha said:
"Great Seer!
This is the wrong time; this is the wrong place."
At that time, that consciousness is formless and invisible, lacking any radiance.
Thus, the element of consciousness does not attain detachment from desire in this place, nor does it fail to arise within the conditioned.
If it were so, then all sentient beings—those with merit and those without merit—would all attain nirvāṇa.
Such is that meaning; Great Seer, you should know this.
If that consciousness-mind thinks in such a way, that consciousness possesses such superior power; this should be understood as such, and not as the power of the body.
As for what is called "consciousness," why is it named "consciousness"?
"Because it accumulates, it is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); because it discerns, it is called wisdom (*jñāna*); therefore, it is termed 'consciousness-consciousness.
Such is the meaning of consciousness; the Great Sage should know this.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Protecting all enemies, they gather to create afflictions;
whether with knowledge or without it, delusion and wisdom act in conjunction."
Views, pride, ignorance, and so forth— All are known by consciousness;
These three are not separate from consciousness, Nor do they exist elsewhere apart from it.
One should speak of consciousness as being in pairs: a single wheel is not a chariot, nor can two wheels travel alone;
when the spokes and rim are joined together, these two wheels are in correspondence.
Furthermore, bound by ropes, it is thus made into a moving vehicle.
So too is this body-vehicle: through the conjunction of the elements (dhātu) and the further conjunction of the sense-faculties (indriya), consciousness perceives that body-vehicle.
The convergence of veins, joints, and so forth; bound by the throat and the roots of the vessels;
hair, bones, teeth, and the head; covered by nails and skin;
the sides, the location of the intestines, the stomach, as well as the heart, abdomen, and lungs.
The union of all these, being complete, is therefore called the body (*kāya*).
With consciousness as the king and the body as the chariot, moving and sitting within this body-chariot, one knows all phenomena;
such is what is termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
This consciousness is subtle, formless, and without substance; it is not visible.
Consciousness does not possess color; it is not a color such as blue or the like."
Within form there are no sense organs; if consciousness were separated from the organs, there would be no objective realm.
Whether it be agitation and fear within a person’s mind, or doubt and deliberation—all such things are the power of consciousness.
At that time, the Rishi Vyāsa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the fundamental nature of all sentient beings?”
How is one born into the heavenly realm?
How is one born into the realm of hungry ghosts?
How is one born into the animal realm?
How is one born in hell?
How does one produce roots of goodness?
Which roots of goodness lead to birth among the devas?
By what karma is one born among animals?
By what karma is one born among hungry ghosts?
By what karma is one born in the hells?
The Buddha said:
"Great Seer!
You should listen attentively; I shall speak for you."

If ordinary beings who have regressed from their original nature generate merit, this dharma is known by the All-Knowing One; it is not a realm known by those possessing the five supernatural powers, nor can it be known by devas, Brahmās, or Akaniṣṭha deities—it is a realm known only by the All-Knowing One.
This Dharma is not even known by the śrāvakas; how much less could others know it?

Great Seer, you should know that if my disciples, the śrāvakas, who have already abandoned the three impurities and realized the sphere of knowledge of the first fruit, are unknown to all the other great devas and devātidevas, then it is not something you, Great Seer, can know, nor can you know even a small portion of it.
When he had spoken thus, the seer Vyāsa immediately reflected in his mind and thought to himself:
"Birth and death have deceived me.
Having thought this, he prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata and said:
“World-Honored One!
My body is now old, decrepit, and broken; it lacks mindfulness, cannot attain the fruit, and cannot bear the heavy burden of bodhi.”

I now take refuge in the World-Honored One, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha that has transcended the three realms of existence. From this day forth until the end of my life, I shall observe these three refuges; and it is the same for all my disciples as well.
I only pray, World-Honored One,
that you will skillfully explain this for me, so that my retinue may obtain great and wholesome benefit.
The World-Honored One is the sun of omniscience, which dispels the darkness of afflictions.
“I only pray, World-Honored One,
that you will explain this intrinsic nature— the intrinsic nature of sentient beings— concerning their falling away and being reborn among the devas.
The Buddha said:
"Great Seer! Now is the very time; I shall speak for you.

Great Seer, you should know that if a person gives flowers and fragrant garlands with a mind that delights in practice and is endowed with faith, upon the end of life they will be reborn in the Heaven Adorned with Garlands."
Furthermore, O Great Sage!
When a person is about to die, their body emits a fragrant scent like that of incense from flowers.
Furthermore, when they are about to die, they see above them flower-nets of various colors being scattered upon them.
At that time, his kinsmen, parents, brothers, and various relatives held flowers and incense in their hands to make offerings to him, wailing and weeping in grief.
At that time, the person’s complexion becomes oily and lustrous; his gaze does not flicker, and his hands and feet remain straight as he passes away.
As he is about to die, he perceives superior signs: namely, he sees mounds, sees garlands and ornaments, and sees hundreds of thousands of beautiful women surrounding a celestial palace.
Having seen this, that person spoke to his brothers, kinsmen, and others, saying:
"In my dream, I saw a mound of various kinds of precious jewels, various ornaments, and scattered flowers of many sorts."
"If that sick person speaks thus, one should know that by this sign they will, at the end of life, be reborn in the Maṇidhara (Garland-Adorned) Heaven.
When that person is about to die, they see their parents in union in the bedchamber; having seen this, they are immediately reborn."

Furthermore, at that time, the gods adorned with garlands engage in sexual desire through the union of two organs, no different from men in Jambudvīpa; however, they possess one superior quality: they do not emit impurity.
When their minds desire to arise and they mutually recognize one another, their bodies then unite; a wind of passion emerges, and they experience sensual pleasure.
At that very moment, they remain within the womb of the celestial maiden for seven days.
When the seven days had passed, he was born from the right side.
At the very moment of his birth, there appeared a divine fragrance, most excellent and lovely, and various flowers were bound together into a garland that grew upon his chest.
At that time, there was also a sublime fragrance that pervaded and filled one yojana, spreading everywhere with the wind.

At that time, furthermore, garlands of various colors appeared—namely, white, black, yellow, red, the color of lapis lazuli, the color of Jambu-river gold, the pure and exquisite color of the padma lotus, various mixed colors, the color of copper, and the color of fire.
Such a wondrous garland does not wither or fade until death, and it is always imbued with a sublime fragrance.
For this reason, it is called "Adornment of Garlands."
"In that celestial palace adorned with garlands, there is a wondrous heavenly tree, neither too tall nor too short; its sap is extremely sweet, with a flavor like nectar."
Its branches hang downward and are further purified; various groves of trees gather together in every place.
Those trees bear fruit, a combination of eight qualities, endowed with celestial flavor.
The size and shape of those fruits are like those of the *piṇḍa* fruit. Whatever food those devas think of in their minds, they obtain all of it from within those fruits according to their thoughts.
It should be understood that when those devas eat such fruits, it is not called "morsel-food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
"In those places, thorns are far removed and they are adorned with exquisite flowers.
Furthermore, there are places with lush, soft green grass;
and there are places entirely covered with golden sand, from which golden horns protrude."
Furthermore, there are resting places where various kinds of bedding and furnishings appear spontaneously.
There are also celestial maidens, pure and stainless, adorned with exquisite garments; they raise a single eyebrow in playful smiles, their bodies graced by diverse and magnificent attire.
Furthermore, in that place, there is the foremost and supreme bliss, complete whether walking or standing.
There, the lifespan of those devas is two hundred years; when their life is about to end, five signs appear.
What are these five?
First, the heart of the tree upon which that deity relies withers; its branches droop and curl downward, and its flowers lose their fragrance.
Second, the deity finds no joy or pleasure in that tree.
Third, their flower garlands wither;
fourth, the cool celestial breezes turn into hot sensations;
fifth, the celestial maidens feel compassion and all become sorrowful, speaking these verses in unison:
“Abounding in celestial sweet fruits, rich with various divine trees,
and filled with many heavenly maidens— this supreme and wondrous place of celestial bliss—
once the merit of one’s heavenly fortune is exhausted, one must abandon it and depart.”
"Those celestial maidens surrounded the deva-son and raised a great cry, proclaiming these words:
'Impermanence is most evil; it possesses no compassion.'"
"Thus, this deva-son, possessing a heart of affection yet lacking mastery over his own life, shall pass away from this place; may the celestial youth be swiftly reborn among humans.
Having spoken these words in her distress, the celestial maiden, the entire body of that deva-son began to burn with fever.
Once the fever has broken out, his entire body is set ablaze; a single flame arises and he immediately retreats from that place—though his body is burning, he does not experience suffering.
Having retreated from there, he then sees human parents in union.
Having seen this, he was immediately conceived.
"Great Seer, you should know: when that Devaputra Maṇḍanavyūha was born, how did he dwell in the womb?"
When he dwells within his mother’s side, there appear extraordinary signs:

the mother craves fragrances, delights in flower garlands, takes pleasure in various fruits, green groves, and clusters of trees; her mind is at ease, she is fully endowed with all forms of joy, and her body knows no fatigue.

Furthermore, because that son of merit dwells within the treasury, there are further auspicious signs: he may dream of cities with various precious goods for trade, and of various flower garlands strewn along the streets and alleys.
It should be known that his mother possesses such signs.
Furthermore, Great Seer!
When this youth has passed away from the Mālyālaṃkāra heaven and is born among humans, he will conceive a feeling of superior love upon seeing garlands.

They delight in wearing few white garments; their physical complexions are exceptionally radiant, yet their minds lack wisdom. They do not refrain from excessive lust and take pleasure in much frivolous amusement. Whether walking, standing, or otherwise moving, they are always swift and rapid. They enjoy visiting places of entertainment and have a fondness for fine clothing. They cherish groves and forests, and upon seeing the wealth of others, they employ various stratagems in their longing to acquire it.
Great Seer, you should know that when a celestial being adorned with garlands falls from the heavenly realm and is reborn among humans, such are their signs.
*Vyāsapraśna Sūtra*, Volume I;
*Vyāsapraśna Sūtra*, Volume II.
Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei:
"Furthermore, Great Seer, you should also know the signs of birth and decline pertaining to the Four Great Heavenly Kings."
Thus it is, Great Seer!

If one gives rise to a heart of compassion for the poor or for the sick, providing them with clothing, food, or whatever medicine is required for their illness at the appropriate time, in order to eliminate the suffering of cold.
One plants trees along the roads and lanes so that travelers may sit and rest;
one constructs ponds, wells, ditches, and water channels to provide for all.
In this manner, with a mind of faith and a heart of joy, one bestows gifts upon those people.

By virtue of these causes and conditions of wholesome karma, when they are about to die, their bodies are free from filth and impurity, nor are they emaciated; the color of their bodies does not change, and they are neither greasy nor putrid. No part of their body experiences suffering or affliction, their voices do not fail, and all their kinsmen and relatives gather together.

Because there is no distraction, one does not experience anxiety or distress, suffers neither hunger nor thirst, does not have the limbs contract or stretch, undergoes no painful affliction, and does not lose control over excrement or urine.
Because their sensory spheres are unimpeded, they experience neither sorrow nor suffering, and their faculties do not decay.
Such people are thus fully satisfied with all forms of happiness and do not die in distress.
When they relinquish the body, their conscious mind is joyful as they behold the Four Heavenly Kings and the hosts of devas in the groves where they sport and delight.

Having seen the celestial hosts, the corpse’s complexion was like that of a living lotus flower, and its mouth emitted a fine fragrance—a scent like that of asafoetida—while various floral scents wafted with the wind to permeate the corpse.
The consciousness of that deceased person sees the parents approaching their place of birth in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
At that time, the father among the gods is wandering and sporting in a place of play and pleasure; a desire arises, and with his right hand he touches the area below the navel of a celestial maiden.
Due to this tactile contact, consciousness takes refuge within the womb; when seven days have fully elapsed, hair appears and it is complete with all adornments, and a celestial youth is born.
Upon birth, he immediately knows desire and is capable of everything—jesting, laughing, singing, and dancing.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!

In the abodes of those gods of the Four Great Kings, all the palaces have floors made of pure gold; they are adorned with various ornaments and diverse colors, their carvings and decorations distinct and clear. Within these celestial palaces dwell hundreds of thousands of goddesses, and there are hundreds of thousands of trees with exquisitely adorned branches. There is a wind that accords with their wishes, which touches their bodies so they experience joy."
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
The abodes of the hosts of the Four Great Kings have level and well-proportioned city moats; their cities are square, measuring eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and breadth."

Great Seer, you should know that in that grove there are celestial precious jewels serving as lamps for illumination; exquisite, fine silks clothe the trunks of the trees, and banners are suspended from their branches.

The trees were exceedingly supple; when the devas saw them, love and joy arose in their hearts. Within that grove, the blended sounds of flutes, hand-clapping, lutes, drums, and other instruments resounded from within those caves.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!

By the power of various foods, those celestial youths—namely, the celestial rice of 'lump-food' (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) with its excellent fragrance—are able to generate celestial strength, being fully endowed with the merits of fragrance, color, taste, and so forth."
There is a type of non-glutinous rice called Lotus Radiance (*padmaprabhā*), which ripens spontaneously; it is as sweet as nectar and possesses a perfect harmony of various colors and flavors.

There are two food platters: one is a golden platter and the other is a jewel platter. Whatever food and drink those deva sons require, and in whatever manner, all such foods and drinks appear within the platters.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
At that time, the *mukharī* juice produced within those vessels immediately transforms into flowers named *aśoka*.
They possess a fine fragrance; their juice is clear and cool, and drinking it brings refreshing bliss."
Furthermore, that fragrance causes the celestial youths to become intoxicated with joy and find perfect contentment.
"Moreover, O Great Sage!

Surrounding the palaces of those four great princes, there are always exquisite flower garlands; many wonderful flowers adorn the palace pillars, and these pillars—made of gold, jewels, and diamonds—adorn the palaces."
There are superior celestial trees, with *sāla* and *śīrṣa* creepers climbing up their branches.
There are palaces adorned with couches, bedding, and furnishings supported by hundreds of thousands of pillars.
Within them, sixty thousand celestial maidens walk and sit, making those palaces magnificent and exquisite.

Her sublime physical form and every movement were worthy of being gazed upon; her body was adorned with the radiance of celestial garments, and she was graced by a wondrous voice and the charm of bracelets and anklets. Possessing exquisite fragrance and beauty, she was in harmony with the mind of desire, her body exceedingly supple.

Singing, dancing, and playful laughter are constantly uninterrupted; they possess great charm and grace, and as pairs join together, they produce exquisite sounds that harmonize with the notes of flutes.
Such are the celestial palaces of those gods, fully endowed with these qualities.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
The pillars of those celestial palaces are interspersed with gold and jewels, and silk banners are suspended from them, hanging down everywhere.
Furthermore, Great Seer!"
Those Four Great Kings experience supreme sensual pleasures.

Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, Virūḍhaka, and Kuvera—these Four Great Kings, within their palaces, produce sounds of joyful laughter, song, dance, and chanting; they are satiated with celestial food, their faculties are filled with delight, and a virtuous and loving intention arises within them.
In that place, all supreme delights are fully provided.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!

Among the hosts of the Four Great Kings Heaven, the divine youths have long, straight arms that are neither coarse nor slender; they walk like intoxicated elephants, possess the strength of men, and their supple bodies are endowed with celestial marks."
When those devas move about, a sublime fragrance permeates for one yojana.
Furthermore, Great Seer,
their lifespan is five hundred celestial years, and they do not suffer premature death or injury.
There, they experience every kind of supreme pleasure; opening their eyes, they behold signs of delight and affection.

Those gods have many places for play—namely, the place called Subhagākā, the Kadamvaka and Vimāra, the place of the King of Forests Adorned with Radiance, the Śanaka and other such sites of superior amusement—and in such first-rate fragrant places, they enjoy themselves with joyful minds.
After those devaputras have traversed that place, the steps are interspersed with flowers, pearls, gold, and jewels;
these steps are square, exquisitely adorned, and are called the Jewel-Bead Steps.
Hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens sing with exquisite voices, and jewels and musical instruments spontaneously produce sounds as they enjoy manifold sensual pleasures.
When their merit is exhausted and their lives come to an end, certain signs appear:
first, they lose their radiance; they no longer smell fragrant flowers; and they no longer hear the sublime voices of the *kalaviṅka* and *koyaṣṭi* birds or the celestial maidens.
"Great Seer, you should know that furthermore, among the celestial hosts,
those young devas do not go to their respective palaces on certain days when they have gathered in the assembly hall of the celestial palace."

Though there were hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, necklaces produced from trees, and exquisite, superior flowers, and though the forest was filled with the calls of cuckoos and the songs of desire-birds, his heart felt no joy; he wandered and turned about upon the ground.
His garments were soiled and greasy, and his body was extremely hot; looking about with sorrowful anguish, he rolled upon the ground.
He found no joy in the flower-canopied pavilion, and sweat poured from his body.
His eyes were always open, whereas now they blink and gaze;
he moves and turns like a fish cast out of water, scorched by the sun, tossing and turning as he lies alone upon the ground.
Upon seeing this, the celestial maidens all came forward to surround him; they grieved together in detail, wailing with one voice, and spoke thus:
"Alas! Beloved one, where do you wish to go?"

How unexpected is this body, adorned with the foremost of various ornaments, supple, diverse and stainless, with a broad and expansive chest, lovely shoulders, a straight and upright form, and a body so tender?
"How unexpected! Having always delighted in various places for play and sport, why do you now suddenly abandon me and leave the celestial palace? Where do you intend to go?
After those celestial maidens had lamented thus, they spoke again in verse:
"Created by various virtuous minds, The celestial trees are wonderfully adorned;..."
In this abode of the Four Great Kings, there is an abundance of food, drink, and joy.
With its four pillars standing in harmony, it is a supreme realm for gods of merit,
filled with beloved celestial maidens and rich in splendor, virtue, and gladness of heart.
"Why do you suddenly loathe impermanence, causing us to abandon this and depart?
Thus surrounded by those celestial maidens, they wailed aloud with broken voices and drooling mouths; weeping together and speaking together, they were pitiable and worthy of compassion.
Those celestial maidens spoke these words; then, moving away to a distance, they extended their right arms, gathered flowers, and scattered them, saying:
"Go to the good realms! You, go to the good realms!"
"Go toward the realm of humans, to the ground that is a place for generating merit, and plow it with the plow of faith.
One should know that when those gods, whose bodies are thus constituted, hear this as they are about to die, they reflect in this way and realize for themselves that their own bodies are dying.
Experiencing extreme anguish, his entire body becomes steaming hot.
Because of this heat, his body melts away like a drop of ghee; within that cemetery where he died, it completely dissolves and perishes, and his physical form withers.
A "sweeping wind" arises, blowing that celestial body into a thousand fragments; these fine particles disperse and pervade the void.
When one is about to pass away from that realm and receive a human body, one sees the parents of Jambudvīpa in union.
Having seen this, they experience joy and delight and are born in that very place.

Immediately upon taking birth, certain signs appear in their mother: namely, she laughs with joy; she desires superior food and has no liking for meat; she delights in wearing red garments and radiant clothes; she enjoys seeing places where crowds of people gather; and she conceives a feeling of exceptional affection toward her siblings and others.
While within the womb and between the ribs, he experiences no suffering or affliction; there is no spittle or saliva, nor any malice, and no bodily illness.
While remaining within that womb, his hands are fully developed, and only then is he born.
"Once he is born, he is handsome and fair of countenance; those who see him love and cherish him.
As he grows, his heart rejoices upon hearing of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings."

They practice generosity and precepts, yet they drink alcohol until intoxicated; their minds are constantly drowsy while their bodies remain plump and fresh, always adorning themselves with various fragrances.

They cherish forest groves and pleasure gardens, their hearts being full of lustful defilements; their own sense faculties delight in being near women, and they frequently consume food, taking pleasure in fine and delicious meals.
Having constantly practiced song and music, their bodies are glossy and supple, neither too dark nor too pale, and their eyes are like blue lapis lazuli.

Great Seer, you should know that such is the natural disposition of those who have passed away from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and been reborn among humans; such is the characteristic of the continuity perfumed by their former state in the realm of the Four Great Kings.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!

If there are sentient beings who abandon killing, possess pure faith, practice generosity, and have desisted from stealing; if they give as alms *khādaniya*, *bhojaniya*, fruits, *harītakī*, and other necessary items such as clothing, wealth, jewels, gold, and so forth; and if, with a heart of joyful faith and delight, they make offerings with various flowers and worship stūpas and temples, presenting these gifts and offerings."

At the time of death, their bodies will not decay or rot; they will be free from grease, filth, excrement, and foul odors. Their minds will give rise to joy as they personally recollect the roots of goodness they have cultivated throughout their lives.

When one is about to die, certain signs appear: the face is like the color of gold; the nose is straight and not crooked; the mind is unmoved and undisturbed; there is no gasping for breath from the throat, nor coughing, nor labored breathing; the body does not burn with fever; the sense faculties do not deteriorate; the joints and veins do not fail; the body experiences no suffering or distress; while lying on the bed, the body does not twist or turn; and the voice does not break.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
Such sentient beings may die of fever, or die from poisoning, or climb trees for flowers and fruits and fall from them to their deaths, or eat fine food that they cannot digest and thus die."

Desiring to abandon the aggregates, his internal consciousness travels to behold the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven adorned with various jewels, gold, and diamonds interspersed in every part; there, the palace gates are decorated with the forms of golden fish and makaras.
Upon the gate-towers are golden banners with various musical instruments that strike against one another, producing beautiful sounds that gladden the heart.
The forest is adorned with excellent trees possessing various branches and fruits, namely the udumbara, kasa-ra, and candana.
The ground was smeared with fragrant liquid as if with mud; it was adorned with golden paintings and white pearl garlands hung everywhere beneath the trees.
The earth was everywhere soft, always magnificent, and pure at all times.
Fine golden sand is spread across the ground, and garlands of lamps made of celestial pearl-flames encircle it.

There are many celestial maidens, their dwelling places adorned with divine light, constantly singing heavenly songs with exquisite melodies. Adorned behind their elbows, they wear necklaces upon their chests, half-necklaces, armlets, finger-rings, and conch-shell earrings—celestial maidens of various ornaments, upright and beautiful.

“Great Seer, you should know that at that time, the sons of the gods among the hosts of the Heaven of the Thirty-three will be sporting and enjoying themselves, experiencing various sensual pleasures. As they wander through the groves of those pleasure grounds, love and affection will arise in their hearts.”

With his merit-consciousness, he sees the sons and daughters of the gods seated together in that celestial realm; his heart feels joy and delight, and he is swiftly reborn there—like a string threading beads, where the pulling of the string causes the beads to follow—it is not born through any other path.
At the very moment of birth, a flower appeared in the hand of that celestial woman.
Upon seeing it, she knew she had a son; she then presented the flower to her husband, saying:
"My lord, you have now gained a son; you may well rejoice."
When those devas saw this, their hearts were filled with even greater joy, for they knew that his wife had obtained a celestial youth.
Thus, the two devas felt great delight in their hearts.
In this way, when the seven days were complete, the youth’s long hair was curled and waving, pure and stainless, and he was fully adorned with celestial garments.
Before that deva was born, during the seven days [prior], he reflected thus:
"I have passed away from such-and-such a place and been born in this heavenly realm; such-and-such were my parents, and I performed wholesome karmic actions."
Reflecting thus, he gives rise to an extreme state of joy; once joy has arisen, desire is set to manifest, and where there is desire, there is delusion.
That one who delights in desire sees from afar the celestial palaces and places of divine play and pleasure.
Having seen this, and desiring to obtain it, he immediately went toward that place of sport, walking like a rutting elephant.

His arms were like the trunks of elephants—thick, round, slender, and long; his chest was level and upright; his arms were golden in color; and while his upper and lower bodies were broad, his waist was slender.
In his movements he was deliberate and circumspect; his profound mind was courageous and resolute.

His waist was like the grip of a bow, his spine was straight and level, and his two thighs were full and fleshy like banana trees. He was well-versed in the celestial laws, and his beard and whiskers were short and fine.

The celestial fragrance is most exquisite; their skin is thin and reddish like the shell of a melon, and their bodies are fragrant and pure. They possess sovereign ornaments which they take to adorn themselves.

The devas are free from the suffering of illness, their bodies bear a virtuous scent, and they wear wondrous celestial garments. Their physical forms are exceptionally sublime as they adorn themselves with celestial flowers, proceeding in succession through the palaces.
"There he saw a certain masterless celestial maiden and a celestial youth, both of whom were surrounded and attended by all [the other deities], who spoke these words:
'Noble son!'"
Welcome, welcome, noble son! This is your palace;
I am without a husband, having been long separated from my husband, and am left alone with this boy.
I am currently young in years and endowed with exquisite beauty; I am worthy of being honored. My breasts are like golden jars, and my face has the color of a fully blossomed lotus.
My body moves like lightning amidst the clouds—so upright and pleasing to behold.
"I am a celestial maiden; I now offer myself to you for worship and service.
This place of play and delight is adorned with many branches and hearts from the Pāriyātra, Kūṭaśālmali, and Kurabaka trees—soft, pleasing, and beautifully ornamented."
"Sixty thousand celestial maidens provide entertainment here; now they shall entertain and serve the Holy Son. All other palace chambers are likewise not empty.
Therein were lutes, drums, flutes, and other musical instruments; various sounds and celestial fabrics served as adornments, and lion thrones appeared spontaneously.

"Having seen those various adornments and exquisite banners and canopies, just as a king who has received his consecration sits upon a lion throne, so too does that celestial youth sit upon a lion throne."
Once he had sat down, delightful sounds issued from all the musical instruments, and a voice proclaimed throughout all the signs:
"This virtuous being has performed meritorious deeds in Jambudvīpa and has come to be born here in this celestial palace."
He said to the goddess, "Come, come! Approach this place quickly;
you may provide entertainment and delight, and skillfully perform songs and dances for this devaputra—one who cultivated roots of goodness among human beings."
Once these words had been spoken, sixty thousand celestial maidens took flowers with both hands within that grove; they were adorned with exquisite fragrances.
They wore the finest heavenly garments called *tūṇīra*, which were light and fine, and they wore anklets made of the most excellent jewels that produced a wondrous sound.
Thus these women approached him to serve and make offerings.
Those celestial maidens were upright and lovely, like the new moon;
their faces were like lotuses, and their fragrance was like that of the *aśoka* flower.
Thus, the woman approached the youth and spoke these words:
"In this way, noble son!
I shall provide and supply you with everything you require, according to your needs."
"This is what the youth has obtained through the accumulated power of his own roots of goodness and is encompassed by his own merit; thus he now experiences celestial pleasures here.
It is even so, O Great Seer!"

Accompanied by celestial youths and maidens, they frequent the various groves within the Nandana gardens of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, such as the White-Robed Rock where there is supreme radiance, the Saptaparṇa forest, the Khadiraka, the Tālavana, the ponds, springs, and flowing streams, the Aṭavaka with its wondrously colored and beautiful flowers, the Pāriyātra, and the Kukkutārāma. In these places of play and delight, it is supremely cool and pleasant; therein no fierce or evil winds exist.

In various places within those forests, there are many birds with diverse and wondrous songs; there are many celestial flowers and an abundance of celestial fruits, all of which possess exquisite fragrances.
Lamps are made of various precious gems, such as lapis lazuli, musāragalva, and agate.

Furthermore, there are swarms of bees and various *kūṣmāṇḍa* birds intoxicated with passion; there are various birds with exquisite voices, including the *parabhṛta* and the *garuḍa*. These birds have blue throats, their bodies are variegated with wonderful jewels, and they possess long, magnificent beaks of lapis lazuli. They produce various sounds and the most beautiful songs, such as the *sātālī*.
In that grove there are various flowers of diverse colors interspersed, adorning the ground.
There, those celestial youths enjoy all manner of sensual pleasures in such a place.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
In the grounds of the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, there is a wondrous pool of water, as cool and clear as the moon, possessing the eight qualities, pure and stainless."
Furthermore, there are exquisite, hundred-petaled lotuses in full bloom, radiant and flourishing; the banks of the pond are adorned with jewel-trees, and flowers fall upon the ground.
Such is this water of subtle and wondrous merit, wherein devas and devīs sport together in harmony. In those places of play, everything accords with their hearts' desires.
If food is required, various precious vessels emerge, interspersed with diverse jewels, wherein all that is needed is fully provided.
The color and fragrance of the food are white, like the kunda flower, the kumuda flower, or the color of snow; they are endowed with both exquisite color and fragrance.

The celestial maidens poured and offered food to the youth Zhangfengtian; having eaten their fill, he was at peace and comfortable, and it was immediately digested, free from the three defects of pungent, astringent, and bitter flavors.
Those who eat in this manner partake of the unsurpassed celestial food called *sudhā*, which they take from that platter and consume according to what they have obtained through their own karma.

Great Seer, you should know that if a person gives a gift with a defiled mind, the retribution they obtain is likewise so. It is like a single plate of food where the morsels differ in color: some morsels are red, some are yellow, and some are of other colors.
Their bodies are clothed in a single kind [of garment] and achieve a single color, yet the food in their bowls is diverse and not the same.
Thus it is, Great Seer!
If a person, after having given a gift, feels regret and mental fever, that karma will result in a reward where the color of the food is inferior.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!

Among the Thirty-three Gods there is a place of play and delight called Śirīṣakañcana. It is adorned with various trees and blossoming branches, where hundreds of thousands of diverse celestial trees converge. The ground is pure like crystal, stainless and soft."
Furthermore, there are celestial trees, fully endowed with flowers and fruits.
Such a place is where those free from desire dwell in the pure Śirīṣaka grove; it is not a place where celestial maidens dwell in this most excellent and wondrous Śirīṣa-blue pleasure grove.
In all the groves there are always beautiful flowers, and in these flowering groves there are always devas who speak below [the trees].

"Great Seer, you should know that among my śrāvakas and disciples, the most excellent is the Elder Gavāmpati. Born into the Brahmin caste, he dwells with his mind absorbed in dhyāna, with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion. His eye of samādhi has opened, and abiding in the samādhi of loving-kindness, for seven days he remains without inhaling or exhaling."
Great Seer, you should know that once he had entered the samādhi of loving-kindness at that time, if his mind required wind, there was a breeze; if he did not require it, there was no breeze.
When the earth becomes a single flame at the end of the kalpa’s conflagration, not even a portion of his body as small as a mustard seed can be burned.
Even if Mount Sumeru were to fall upon his body, it would be made to rest upon each of his joints, unable to cause him any movement.

Furthermore, Nanda and Upananda, the two evil dragon kings, possess a fierce and blazing power of venom; with such evil power and poison, they can shake Mount Sumeru by merely exhaling their breath, and with such venomous power, they can cause the waters of the four great oceans to become salty.
"Great Seer, you should know that such a powerful and evil venomous dragon king can be rendered non-venomous through the power of the Gābhapati-samādhi.
Furthermore, Great Seer!"
At that time, the Elder Gavāmpati was walking about at the Śīrṣaka Garden for recreation.

Those celestial maidens possessed a powerful mind of lustful passion; either while wandering for play, they arrived at that place, and upon seeing the Elder Gavāmpati, they conceived a heart of love and faith. They scattered offerings of celestial māndārava flowers, jātisumana flowers, and the like, and with palms joined, they paid him homage.

Furthermore, the devaputras of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven surrounded and made offerings to the Elder Gavāmpati, presenting him with celestial food and celestial nectar to satisfy him, making such offerings to him every single day.

Ghapati wandered through the depths of that forest where the tree branches swayed, expounding for those devas the gāthās, udānas, nidānas, itivṛttakas, jātaka-s, vaipulya-s, avadānas, dharmas, vinaya, sūtras, upadeśas, and apadeśas.
