Having caused those devas to hear them and thereby giving rise to faith, joy, and delight, he remained in those celestial and wondrous palaces, practicing dhyāna, reciting, wandering, and dwelling there; he also frequented the Śiśumāra pleasure grounds.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
Among the Thirty-three Gods there is the Sudharmā Hall, the assembly place for the celestial hosts.

Great Seer, you should know that the pillars of the Sudharmā Hall number eighty-four thousand; those pillars are all made of gold-jewels, vajra, musāragalva, karketana, and agate. Exquisite sandalwood rafters run along them above, with the wondrous sounds of tinkling bells and garlands, and the ground is covered with golden sand."
Great Seer, you should know that in that Hall of Good Dharma, celestial silk banners hang down, jeweled victory banners are erected, and streamers are suspended above.
Furthermore, there is the sound of music: lutes, zithers, flutes, large drums, small drums, hand-clapping, conch shells, and the beautiful tones of flutes and whistles.

The hands of the deva kings and deva maidens are like exquisite flowers; their softness is like the core of tree branches. They hold one another’s hands, their hearts filled with love and joy, their mouths always curved in smiles.
Those celestial youths and celestial women experience such pleasures in this way.
"Great Seer, you should know that in that Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā), where many gods assemble, the ground is inlaid with various kinds of precious jewels."

That ground is as green and lustrous as beryl; it is smooth and stainless like a pure mirror. It abounds with celestial flowers and various kinds of fragrant powders. It is far removed from such afflictions as wind, sun, blue insects, mosquitoes, and gadflies; there is no sleep, indolence, or yawning.

In that Hall of Good Dharma (*Sudharmā*), the wind-blown windows, multi-storied pavilions, and wall surfaces are adorned with various interlaced patterns; their shapes are like half-moons and their forms resemble ox-eyes, all covered by a celestial lattice canopy.

The exquisite gateway of the owl’s tail is vast and expansive; it possesses winds of pleasant touch, is adorned with jeweled garlands, strewn everywhere with wonderful flowers, and filled with fragrant perfumes.

It abounds with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens who laugh and play with amorous intent; they are free from faults such as jealousy or strife, and are mutually immersed in desire. Their love is firm and steadfast, and their cheeks are pure and stainless like the orb of the moon or a polished mirror.
"The nature of the celestial maidens is to adorn their faces by applying fragrant pigments and colors to their cheeks and foreheads; they take delight together in the sounds of celestial songs.

Great Seer, you should know that in the four directions and four corners of that Sudharmā Hall, the four galleries are vast and wide, with many groves of trees that are deep, dense, and dark as clouds, and filled with various kinds of flowers."

In this place of amusement, such groves extend for a hundred *yojanas* and are adorned in every part with various forms of beauty. There are golden lotuses, and scattered flowers are spread across the ground. Furthermore, there are various subtle and exquisite songs, and many kinds of trees; these trees are named Kucanada, Pāriyātra, and Kovidāra, and such trees abound everywhere, serving as its adornment.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!

In that Sudharmā Hall, there are all manner of necessities—gold, jewels, diamonds, mūśala stones, and karava stones—as well as white pearls, lapis lazuli, and so forth. Each of these forms a great heap; they have no owner and are unguarded, being a vast treasury of wealth, gold, and jewels."
All those objects and all those heaps of jewels completely adorn the site of the Hall of Good Dharma; those heaps of jewels are adorned with various colors.

Surrounding that Sudharmā Hall, there are further hundreds of thousands of pleasure grounds for adornment; they are free from heat and free from affliction, and various garments serve to decorate those places.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, delighting in play and fond of playful activities, all gather together in the Sudharma Hall to enjoy themselves and take pleasure."
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
The Sudarśana palace of the Trāyastriṃśa gods is as pure as a moon-mirror, adorned with many fragrant flowers and hanging garlands.

There are a thousand celestial maidens, exquisitely adorned, sporting and enjoying themselves; they cast sidelong glances with alluring eyes, their brows and faces arching like turbulent waves as they travel through the void, their bodies decorated with various kinds of flowers."
The palace of Sudarśana was adorned in this manner; within the palace were many pearl vases, and networks of bells and curtains produced subtle and wondrous sounds as part of its adornment.
Whether it be horses or elephants moving through the palaces, their hooves striking the ground raise up golden dust.

In that place there are many beautiful celestial maidens, their bodies adorned with precious jewels that emit crimson light; whether they sing, embrace, or grasp the garments [of the gods], they cause that place of play to be exceptionally sublime and wondrous.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!

The palace of Sudarśana has sixty thousand pillars. Those pillars are all made of celestial, exquisite gold and jewels; they have heads of *vaiḍūrya* and *vajra* gems, with various miscellaneous jewels interspersed between them."
Within that palace, it is perfumed by various fragrances such as liquid incense, leaf incense, and aloeswood, as well as by various other excellent and superior scents.
There, in that sublime place, Śakra, the King of Devas, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, holds a vajra-tusk in his hand and enjoys himself in sport upon the jeweled palace.
"Furthermore, Great Seer! The King Indra of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven possesses the strength of nine thousand nāgas.

The arms of King Śakra are like the trunks of celestial elephants; his body is golden in color, bright and pure without stain. His form is well-proportioned, tapering at the waist and broadening toward the shoulders. His joints do not protrude, and his body is solid rather than hollow. His hair curls and turns, pure and stainless; his body emits radiance, and his garments are flowing and long."

Knowing that the *Śakrapraśnīya-śāstra* composed by Indra is capable of refuting contentious treatises, many hundreds of thousands of immeasurable devaputras constantly follow and attend upon him, accompanying him as he wanders through celestial groves, palaces, and pleasure gardens.
His body was entwined with golden cords, and his chest was adorned with celestial, exquisite necklaces or half-necklaces.
His form was sublime and wondrous—neither too slender nor too coarse—with a slender waist and symmetrical thighs.

They constantly partake of white rice and ambrosial nectar; hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens gaze upon them with eyes like flower garlands, their shoulders and cheeks being perfectly formed.
There, intoxicated elephants fan the air with their ears, producing a breeze whose sound is exquisite.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!

The bodily veins of that Great Heavenly King Indrasena do not appear; his fragrance is most excellent and sublime, like the scent of fine flowers, and the voice of that Great Heavenly King is soft and beautiful."

Great Seer, you should know that the Great Heavenly King’s own body possesses a sublime fragrance; even when a celestial white elephant is about to become extremely intoxicated, it awakens and recovers its senses immediately upon smelling the fragrance of the King’s body.
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
As for the height and stature of King Indra’s body, it is equal to the height and stature of the other gods who ride horses.
The color of King Indra’s body is exceptionally sublime; when one beholds his body, even golden images do not appear by comparison."
At that time, the great seer Vyāsa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How rare this is!”
“World-Honored One!
That Great Indra, King Śakra, is indeed most excellent and sublime; it is truly as the World-Honored One—one who is fully endowed with the noble Dharma—has said, and not otherwise.”
The Buddha said,
"Great Seer!
For what reason do you thus praise this impermanent body, the Great Indra, as being rare and wonderful, giving rise to such astonishment in your mind?"

It is like an actor who skillfully fashions various forms of humans, animals, and so forth from lumps of clay; he further binds leaves and other materials, inserts flowers on the outside, and uses various pigments to paint them as military hosts.

Wood is used for mechanical contrivances, which are painted and carved; like a tree producing flowers, these paintings and ornaments provide a magnificent adornment, yet before long the flowers wither.
It is also like placing a lamp wick in a burner and burning it with fire, whereby light is produced;
the body of King Śakra is likewise thus.
"Great Seer, you should know that Aniruddha’s strength, born of his parents, is great.
Great Seer, you should know that even the bodily strength possessed by King Indra is surpassed by the bodily strength of Aniruddha, born of his parents."
"Furthermore, Great Sage!
You should now observe the power of the body and the supernormal faculties of Aniruddha.
When this was said, Aniruddha immediately brought it to mind.
"May the Tathāgata empower me.
Having thought thus, he immediately entered samādhi.

Having entered samādhi, his body became like the color of gold, and there appeared upon his head a new and magnificent crown of heavenly kings, like the color of molten gold; from it hung precious jewels that reached down to his cheeks and shoulders, moving and rubbing against one another.
With a jeweled topknot and blue-black hair, his body was lustrous and possessed a superior radiance; his eyes were like the finest heavenly lapis lazuli, a deep azure in color.
Furthermore, his body and arms were adorned with various jewels, including *maṇi*, *musāra-galva*, *karavīra*, and *sūryakānta* gems.
By the power of his transformations, he caused his body to become thus.
Furthermore, he emitted a celestial fragrance that pervaded the entire assembly, universally perfuming all.
Upon seeing his body, Vyāsa’s mind was moved; he rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, gave rise to a sense of wonder, and cried out in a loud voice:
"Excellent, excellent, my son!
How joyful this is!
Having obtained a human body, my attainment has borne fruit and is not in vain."
I have now come to the presence of the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata has now spoken words corresponding to all-knowledge, enabling me to behold such an unprecedented phenomenon as this.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the great seer Viśvāmitra:
"What do you think?
Between the body of Indra, the king of the Śakras, and the body of the elder Aniruddha—which of these two bodies is superior?"
At that time, the great seer Vyāsa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Compared to the body of King Indra, the body of Aniruddha does not equal even one-hundredth part; it does not equal even one-thousandth part. The body of Aniruddha is fully endowed with the excellence of color.”
The Tathāgata said: "It is so, Great Seer!
Do not give rise to joy; it was by performing meritorious deeds and making such a vow that you obtained that body."
At that time, the great seer Vyāsa and his assembly, their minds filled with joy and opened wide, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We pray that the World-Honored One will further explain the Heaven of the Thirty-three for us."
The Buddha said,
"Great Seer! Śakra,
the King of Devas of the Thirty-three Heavens, has a primary queen named Śacī."

A hundred thousand celestial maidens dwell in the Forest of Joy; various flowers in full bloom radiate light that gathers upon their bodies. Their cheeks are like lotuses, their lips are the color of golden *bimba* fruits, and they wear garments of the finest, most subtle light.

They strolled and wandered with composed gait through the pleasure groves, their ears beautifully adorned with celestial ornaments; their arms were graced with jeweled bracelets and celestial conchs, their bodies decorated with exquisite necklaces and half-necklaces; and on their feet they wore jeweled anklets that produced wondrous sounds like various kinds of music.
Thus they wander through the Nandana Grove; their cheeks are broad and full, and they walk upon the ground strewn with exquisite flowers.
Below the navel and above the private parts, there are fine patterns of hair, and they wear garments of wondrous jewels that emit sounds as they move.
His eyes are blue and wide, open and charming; his hair is long, black, and each strand curls to the right; his nose is prominent and straight.
He is far removed from faults such as anger, envy, and strife; he is entirely free from wrath, frowning, agitation, and turbulence, and his body is without hidden flaws.
"Great Seer, you should know that the queen Śacī possesses a power of desire for pleasure that surpasses even the most excellent places on Mount Meru.
That place is vast and extensive, with many groves of trees whose branches are so thick that they provide dense shade."
A heart of love and joy arose within him. A gentle breeze blew upon the flowers, causing them to sway and scatter their fragrance, which further touched his body.

Śāṇakavāsin’s physical form was neither tall nor short, neither coarse nor slender; his face was as beautiful as a blooming lotus, his mouth emitted a wondrous fragrance, and his skillful speech increased the seeds of the Buddha.

"Great Seer, you should know that all the celestial hosts of the Heaven of the Thirty-three have fragrant bodies and are free from illness; they roam about thus in their pleasure grounds or within their palaces."
"Furthermore, Great Seer!
The lifespan of the gods in the Heaven of the Thirty-three is one thousand years.
When their life there has thus come to its end, you should know that five signs will appear in their celestial palaces that were never present before."
What are these five?
The ground possesses clear water like crystal, which is cool, marked with patterns, and possesses winds with a pleasant touch.
In that place there are many various flowering branches; once one has entered the pool, oily sweat breaks out.
Having seen him thus covered in oiliness and sweat, a sense of doubt arose in her mind; she immediately emerged from the water and hurried toward the forest.
As he walked swiftly, the celestial maiden saw him and followed closely behind, accompanying him.
Having arrived at a tree, he immediately sat down.
Once he was seated, the celestial maiden, overcome with grief and sorrow, let out a sigh; her voice broke in her throat as she asked him thus:
"Noble Son!..."
"Why have you now abandoned me and stayed alone beneath this tree?
What pleasure is there here?
Having spoken thus, the celestial youth addressed the goddess with a voice of sorrowful lamentation:
"I have never, from time immemorial, had any oil or grease emerge upon my forehead.
Having spoken thus, sweat immediately broke out from both his armpits.
When that celestial maiden saw the sweat appear, she abandoned him and departed to a distance.
When he saw that the celestial maiden had departed from his body, a sense of grief and fear arose in his mind, and his inhalations and exhalations became coarse.
Once his breath had become coarse, his heart grew feverish.
Because his heart was thus heated, the exquisite garland upon his head—which had never before withered—now began to fade.
Once their garlands have withered, and their clothes— which were never soiled before— now show signs of grime,
the celestial beings find no pleasure in their beds and seats.
When those goddesses observe such signs, they immediately think to themselves:
"The signs of death have already appeared upon this celestial youth; he is about to perish.
Knowing that he was certain to die and finding his stench unbearable, they immediately moved away from him and stood surrounding him.
Upon smelling its odor, he was filled with pity and lamented with such grief that his voice broke and his mouth could no longer speak properly; he uttered these words: "Alas!

How is it that the Deva of the most supple body, who used to wander through the groves of the pleasure grounds—where in those three celestial realms there are such lotus ponds with ruddy geese, where in the Hall of Good Dharma there are the Forests of Joy, where the waters of the Mandākinī pond are fragrant and pure with royal swans and ruddy geese, where there are many forests of trees named Hastikakṣya, Pārijāta, and Kovidāra, and where in those pleasure spots amidst the various groves many bees provide adornment—he who always roamed these places, has now suddenly abandoned me; where is he going?"
"Once these five signs have appeared, my body will be destroyed and I shall depart.
As those celestial maidens wept in this manner, they wept even more.
Seeing them weeping, his heart was shattered and he was seized by great terror.

His body burned with fever and his eyes wandered in confusion; he was like a traveler on a road who has lost his companions, or like a merchant at sea whose ship has foundered, or like one who has lost a wish-fulfilling jewel, falling to the ground in heart-rending anguish.
Just as a powerful wind can topple a mountain peak, so too does the great wind of impermanence cause the deva-son to fall.

His body becomes intensely hot, and he rolls upon the ground like a young nāga seized by a garuḍa. Stricken with great terror, his entire body trembles, and with palms joined, he speaks to the celestial maiden:
"I am now afflicted by heat; come, come! Rub me with your palm to cool me."
Thus their hearts were distressed and their bodies burned with fever; in this way, both body and mind suffered together.

Those celestial maidens, their hearts scorched by grief and sorrow, remained at a distance; moved by compassion, yet tormented by grief and suffering, they were unable to draw near, nor could they stroke or touch him.
From within the grove of trees, he plucked a branch with its flowers and leaves, extended his hand, and placed it from afar upon the heart of the deva-son, speaking these words:
"Young man, your celestial merit is now exhausted; I pray that you may quickly be reborn in the realm of Jambudvīpa."
Upon hearing this, that deva realized he was certain to die and cried out in a loud voice:
"How tragic! How tragic!"
This realm of the Trāyastriṃśa gods is, in truth, a place of suffering.

Although it is thus endowed with various perfected adornments and places of play and pleasure, where one enjoys all manner of delights within the supreme palaces, and though the minds of many have been bound by attachment to various celestial maidens, they now suddenly find themselves on the path of death. Standing at a distance, they speak these words:
"May you, after death, be reborn in Jambudvīpa."
Having reflected thus many times and having heard those words, that deva attempted to rise from his seat with his whole body; overcome by intense sorrow and suffering, he wept and said:
"Alas, what bitter pain! The Forest of Joy, the Forest of Various Trees, the white-robed stone, and the place for sitting and sporting!"
How excellent are these dharmas: those [trees] such as the lodhra, the pārijāta, this pippala, the mandārava, and the mahāpārijāta.
Such is this palace—the foremost of palaces—with its sturdy door-panels all firmly joined together; yet now I suddenly abandon this celestial palace, losing my mastery and thus departing from it.

"Because their lifespans in the Heaven of the Thirty-three were about to end, they could no longer see their own palaces; they saw only the celestial maidens with their faces turned downward, wiping their eyes with their hands, sighing deeply, and weeping."
That deva, desiring to fall, spoke again in this way:
"I am now about to tread the path of death; why do you wait for me to withdraw from my beloved ones and refuse to speak with me?"
"I am now about to travel the long road of birth and death; O beloved, come quickly and embrace my neck!
From this day forth I shall no longer see you, and you likewise shall no longer see me."
"How truly wretched is this celestial realm! Once the fruits of one's karma are exhausted, it becomes dark and nothing can be seen.
Why is it that when those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three are about to fall away, this place becomes entirely empty?"
"How is it that here in the Heaven of the Thirty-three there are no longer lutes, music, or the clapping of hands?
Why is it that I no longer hear such sounds?

How remarkable that in this Heaven of the Thirty-three—the most beloved of heavens—where the Gandharvas possess such celestial adornment and the ground is as firm as diamond, one might behold the Thousand-Eyed Śakra, King of Devas, and other beings of such merit gathered together there!"
"The *pārijāta* and *kovidāra* trees, and all the flower garlands upon my head—how could they have withered so unexpectedly?

Thus did that falling deva cry out. When the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens heard his voice, they were all filled with sorrow; they took various flowers to adorn themselves and purified their hair and beards.

Śakra, King of Devas, was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial hosts; he was also encircled by the Queen Śacī and the heavenly maidens, as well as Nārada, Citraratha, Pañcaśikha, Tumburu, and others. Amidst the songs and melodies of the celestial gandharvas and the exquisite sounds of divine music, they approached those who were about to enter the path of death and exhibit the five signs of decay.
Having seen this closely, they all felt such compassion that they cried out with one voice:
"How tragic! This evil impermanence has no heart of mercy!"
When Śakra, King of the Devas, saw that those gods were thus about to fall, he spoke in a Brahma-voice:
"All dharmas are like this for us; do not give rise to attachment, but rather sever the heart of craving."
"If one does not sever craving, one will be born in the evil realms.
The other devas likewise spoke with one voice, saying:
"May you go to a good realm and be born among human beings, the land where all sentient beings perform wholesome deeds."
When he had spoken thus, that deva who was about to fall away immediately thought to himself:
"I am indeed falling away.
At once, he joined his palms toward the assembly of devas and spoke to them as follows:
"O all you devaputras of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven!
I pray that you will forgive me, for the time of my departure has arrived.
At that moment, the devaputra drew in his breath and gazed straight ahead; two signs then appeared:
The lotus-petal eyes and all their ornaments completely vanished.

When those devaputras saw that the deva about to fall was divested of his ornaments, they took mandārava flowers, kovidāra flowers, karṇikāra flowers, and others of like kind, and scattered them from afar over his body.
They immediately played celestial music, delighting him with various sounds such as lutes, drums, and flutes.
Having seen such offerings made to his body, although he was destined to fall from the celestial realm, his heart gave rise to joy, and he conceived a longing for Jambudvīpa.
Tears flow from his eyes and his voice becomes coarse as he says:
"The time has come; through the accumulation of karma and dharmas, my life has reached its end.
Once his life has ended and he has died, the *gāhana* wind blows upon that deceased deva.
That wind, with its excellent fragrance, blows them apart.
Once thus dispersed, they immediately depart from the Heaven of the Thirty-three; their location is unknown, they have no fixed abode, and others can neither perceive nor know them.
"Once they have passed away from there, they are born among human beings.

While still in the womb, signs appear in the mother: she delights in laughing, singing, and dancing; her mind takes pleasure in sensual desires and is constantly joyful; she delights in places with flowers, fruits, and groves; she is fondly attached to various multicolored garments and always enjoys food and drink."

Although he dwells within the womb, his mother’s side suffers no pain; he takes no pleasure in improper desires, but his mind delights in fine fragrances and the adornment of flower garlands; when he lies down, he has auspicious dreams and no distorted visions.
"Great Seer, you should know that when those from the Heaven of the Thirty-three fall and are reborn at this time, they possess such signs while dwelling within their mother's womb.
Great Seer, you should know that at that time, the mother is entirely free from all defects of the womb, and subsequently gives birth."

Great Seer, you should know that when the boy was born at that time, his limbs were well-proportioned, his palms were marked with auspicious lines, he was lovely and soft-limbed, his waist was slender, his teeth were closely set, and his body was supple.
Their minds delight in superior merit and desire; by nature they crave sensual matters, their hearts yearn for fine garments, and they take pleasure in forested pleasure groves.

Their bodies possess a sublime fragrance; they are of great wealth and abundant riches, fully endowed with gold and jewels, and born into a noble lineage. They constantly practice giving and precepts;
yet those whose minds are full of desire are born into poor families.
He delights in giving; his complexion is neither dark nor pale, and his hands and feet are even and level. All who see him love and revere him.

By nature he loves to discuss the principles of the Dharma, and his mind is supple. He has little anger, yet he takes pleasure in the wives of others and feels no affection for his own wife or concubines. Toward his kinsmen, brothers, and relatives, his heart is devoid of attachment.
"Great Seer, you should know that it is the very nature of those who fall from the Heaven of the Thirty-three and are reborn among humans to be thus.
When the World-Honored One had finished speaking, the Seer Vyāsa and the entire assembly of seers felt great joy in their hearts and exclaimed:
"Excellent!"
The Vyāsapraśna Sūtra, Scroll II.
